p: Dabhol, also written Dabul, is a small seaport town in the Ratnagiri district of Maharashtra. It lies on the northern and southern sides of the Vashishti River, which also flows by the town of Chiplun. Under the Bahmani dynasty the port was known as Mustafabad and later as Hamjabad before it took its present name. From the 14th to the 16th century it was the principal port of the southern Konkan, trading with ports of the Mediterranean Sea, the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf.

The Russian traveller Afanasy Nikitin, who visited India from 1468 to 1474, found Dabhol a large town and extensive seaport, to which horses from Mysore, Arabia and Khorasan were brought for sale, and which had links with all the major ports from India to Ethiopia. In the 15th and 16th centuries it was an opulent Muslim trading centre, first under the Bahmani sultans and later under those of Bijapur. It was the port with the most convenient access to the Bahmani capital at Bidar, and its fortunes rose with that dynasty; at its height it was arguably the most important port between Chaul and Goa.

That prominence made it a target. In December 1508 a Portuguese expeditionary force under Francisco de Almeida bombarded, sacked and razed the town in the Battle of Dabul, a prelude to the Battle of Diu, though the fort was not taken. The Portuguese tried several more times over the following decades to destroy it; at the last recorded attack, in 1571, the governor was Khwaja Ali Shirazi, and 150 men were killed at Dabhol.

The break-up of the Bahmani state into smaller Deccan sultanates hastened the port's decline. As new capitals were built its position was no longer so favourable, and during the 16th century much commerce moved south to the rising port of Rajapur. Shivaji conquered Dabhol around 1660 and annexed it to the new Maratha kingdom. It passed to Sambhaji, who gave it to Khando Ballal Chitnis as a reward for saving him from drowning in a river in Goa.

The Dabhol vatan is still claimed by descendants of the Chitnis family of Satara, although some descendants of the Shirke family argue that it should be theirs. On the southern side of the town, between the villages of Veldur and Ranavi, stands the Dabhol LNG power plant, which was set up by the company Enron.

notes: The article says the Bahmani ruled the port 'during the 13th to 15th centuries'; I gave no span for Bahmani rule.
The article calls the Bijapur rulers 'Badar sultans' (unclear; perhaps Adil Shahi); I wrote only 'those of Bijapur'.
Nikitin's list of horse sources also has 'Nighostan', which I could not identify and left out.
The article does not say which side lost the 150 men in 1571; I kept its wording.
The article does not explain 'vatan'; I left it unglossed. The last section is short (about 55 words).
